The Andhra Pradesh government has directed officials to evacuate people from flood-prone areas, prioritise vulnerable residents, and deploy disaster response teams in the wake of the cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’.
Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has ordered heightened preparedness across the State, officials said, adding that 4,711 pregnant women will be shifted to safer healthcare facilities.

Health Secretary G. Veerapandian and Health and Family Welfare Commissioner K.V.N. Chakradhar Babu reviewed the preparedness measures during a teleconference with senior officials and district medical authorities on Monday evening.

article_sentences: Cyclone Arnab Live Updates: Odisha and Andhra Pradesh have shut schools, restricted fishing and mobilised rescue teams ahead of Cyclone Arnab's expected landfall on Wednesday, with authorities preparing for heavy rain and destructive winds.

The India Meteorological Department said the cyclone is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam by the forenoon of October 28, with sustained winds of 115-125 kmph and gusts reaching 140 kmph.

Odisha has begun evacuating people from vulnerable areas and deployed rescue teams, while Andhra Pradesh has stationed 15 NDRF teams across affected districts and released Rs 27 crore for relief operations.
The Centre has directed disaster response agencies to ensure minimal loss of life and damage to infrastructure.
Rescue teams from the NDRF, Army, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard have been deployed or kept on standby.

stories.title: China, Pak psyop against Indians? Spurt in fake news amid LAC face-off reports
stories.summary: China, Pak psyop against Indians? Spurt in fake news amid LAC face-off reports
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: From a military briefing falsely linked to Arunachal Pradesh to a counter-terrorism drill passed off as Chinese soldiers frisking Indian troops, Indians are being targeted with fake news on X. The spurt of such posts comes even as reports emerge of face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal.
Is it part of a psyop by Pakistan and China?

Amid reports of face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at multiple points along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh, old videos and misleading visuals and commentary are being circulated on social media, fuelling claims of Chinese incursions and military setbacks for India.
The Indian Army's official fact-checking account on X has been busy busting fake news for the last couple of days.

These misleading posts have emerged against the backdrop of renewed military friction along the LAC, which is not demarcated mutually by India and China, leading to differing perceptions of the boundary.
On October 22, Director General Shatrujeet Kapoor of the Indian-Tibetan Border.
Police (ITBP) said Indian and Chinese troops had faced-off in multiple locations along the LAC since at least July.
Reports had emerged that Chinese troops had been denying Indian forces access to key patrolling points along the LAC in the Taksing area.

It is against this backdrop of ongoing tensions that misleading posts have emerged on X. It is not yet known whether these are part of a coordinated disinformation or psychological operation (psyop) directed by Beijing.
But given China's well-developed cognitive warfare capabilities and its history of alleged disinformation campaigns, the posts warrant caution.
The Indian Army's official fact-checking account has called out certain posts as Pakistan-linked.

In one prominent post, a digitally altered video falsely attributes remarks to Lt Gen Girish Kalia, claiming China has taken control of Asaphila, Longju and Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh and blocked supplies to Indian troops.

stories.headline: A critical fault line
stories.title: A critical fault line
stories.summary: For many in the country, a recent statement by ShatrujeetKapur, the Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), regarding face-off situations along the Chinese border in Arunachal Pradesh served as a revealing exercise. The situation suggests that while the distressing pre-and-post-Galwan Valley episode—which lasted well over four and a half years—is not repeating exactly, a new trap is being set: the “Eastern Ladakh syndrome.” This syndrome refers to the sensitive border friction in Ladakh that began in April–May 2020 and lasted until October 2024. That standoff was resolved following a meeting between Prime Minister NarendraModi and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, where both leaders pledged to work toward a peaceful resolution of the decades-old boundary dispute. In the aftermath of that summit, and during subsequent high-level meetings, matters appeared to be moving toward a resolution. The brutal clashes in the Galwan Valley—fought in steep gorges at dizzying heights of 14,000 to 17,000 feet on the night of June 15–16, 2020—had initially generated hope that an Eastern Ladakh-type crisis could be permanently averted. However, the context of this new syndrome is different. It is not necessarily the immediate repetition of a war-like theater along the borders, but rather the constant, lingering threat that it might happen. In military strategy, the psychological impact of such uncertainty is often greater than actual combat conditions. This syndrome cannot—and should not—be wished away. Today, China is aggressively upgrading its technology-driven military software and hardware. While these advancements are not exclusively India-specific, the fact that India sits in China’s immediate neighbourhood cannot be ignored, especially given past betrayals. It should also not be forgotten that China and Pakistan are all-weather friends who have stood by each other in all seasons. Chinese support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor in May 2025 is a matter of record, opening new vistas of threat for India. China-Pakistan relations are not just standard bilateral relations; they have been further fostered by both countries controlling the occupied territories of Jammu and Kashmir on the other side of the Line of Control (LoC) in the Karakoram range. They are also partners in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which illegally passes through Pakistan-occupied territories of Jammu and Kashmir. That aspect should not be ignored. The ITBP chief did not state anything entirely new; border friction has long existed due to the largely un-demarcated Line of Actual Control (LAC). Nevertheless, his remarks exposed a critical fault line that must be taken seriously, rather than dismissed as a routine occurrence on a borderline where perceptions matter more than ground reality. Addressing troops in Alwar, Rajasthan, the ITBP chief noted, “In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh, and it still continues.” This statement implies that China has returned to the playbook it deployed in eastern Ladakh prior to the full-fledged military standoff of 2020. It reinforces the reality that patrolling in these sensitive sectors remains far from settled. Crucially, the admission that these face-offs are ongoing means the threat is active and demands a more robust response to prevent a repeat of Eastern Ladakh. It should be averted not only physically but also psychologically. Kapur also highlighted the obvious while praising the capabilities of the ITBP’s new combat unit, the ‘Shaurya Commandos,’ for their skills during these face-offs with the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). He unequivocally described China as India’s biggest adversary and the China front as the force’s most difficult assignment. In sensitive matters of national security, neither underplaying nor overplaying a threat is helpful. The intention behind these face-offs matters more than the immediate physical action. Even if PLA troops pitch tents, display banners, and subsequently retreat, these actions should be read as exploratory steps to test India’s response times and military readiness. They serve as a stark reminder of the early days of the 2020 Ladakh crisis, the memories of which remain deeply etched in India’s military and civil psyche. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) provided necessary clarity on the matter. MEA spokesperson RandhirJaiswal observed: “As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns.” He added that both sides continue to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to avoid miscalculation along the LAC, while agreeing to discuss better border management. Domestically, the Arunachal situation has triggered two unhelpful extremes. On one side, certain opposition figures and analysts have rushed to draw alarmist parallels to the 2020 standoff, using the crisis to score political points against the government without realizing that their rhetoric inadvertently aids the adversary and confuses the public. Equally distressing is the counter-narrative from certain retired generals and security commentators who dismiss the entire development as a routine event requiring no alarm. The real picture lies somewhere in between, requiring both context and long-term perspective. As the international landscape shifts—with the US and China actively engaging in new military dialogues between the Pentagon and the PLA—New Delhi must look toward a strategic reset. International observers note that India and China must engage in more frank diplomatic and military talks, keeping trade and bilateral interests functional without letting past conflicts entirely dictate the present. India possesses the capacity to manage this balance. Moving forward, Chinese attempts to manufacture an “Eastern Ladakh syndrome” in the east must be countered through an unyielding combination of sophisticated diplomacy and enhanced military capability.

stories.headline: Khooni Nallah, a part of Kashmir’s highway folklore, set to be bypassed
stories.title: Khooni Nallah, a part of Kashmir’s highway folklore, set to be bypassed
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 26: Khooni Nallah, the blood-soaked ravine etched into Kashmir's highway folklore by rockfalls and fatal accidents, is set to be bypassed by December as work nears completion on the second tube of the Digdol-Panthiyal tunnel along the Srinagar-Jammu National Highway. The 2.6-km northbound tube towards Srinagar, along with an additional 619-metre section towards Kashmir, is scheduled to become operational by December 2026, NHAI Project Director Shubham Yadav told Greater Kashmir. He said the work was on track, with only a 170-metre diversion remaining. The 3.08-km southbound tube towards Jammu was opened in July. The new tube will bypass Khooni Nallah and other vulnerable stretches around Digdol and Panthiyal, where falling rocks and landslides have repeatedly disrupted traffic. The journey from Digdol to the Ramsoo-Magarkote side is expected to take around five minutes. The nearly 5.7-km Digdol-Panthiyal twin-tube project, being built at a cost of Rs 866.37 crore, began in 2022 and uses the New Austrian Tunnelling Method. Each tube has a width of 10 meters, ensuring sufficient space for vehicular movement and enhanced safety standards. MAGARKOTE-PANTHIYAL TUNNEL NEARING COMPLETION Work on the separate 619-metre-long tube, known as the 84 tunnel is nearing completion and it is expected to open to traffic by December, Yadav said. The 870-metre twin tube T5 cut-and-cover tunnel, built with a protective canopy, is already operational. Together, the tubes form a four-lane structure that has shortened the route by around 1.1 km, bypassing much of the landslide-prone Panthiyal stretch between Magarkote and Panthiyal. The tunnel section is part of the larger, multi-kilometre Digdol-Panthiyal complex, aimed at ensuring safer, all-weather connectivity along the Ramban-Banihal corridor while reducing exposure to falling rocks, slope failures and weather-related disruptions. "Earlier, when rocks used to fall and during heavy rains, many people would be forced to wait for days on either side. Now, we can reach from Digdol to the Ramsoo-Magarkote side in just five minutes," said Abdul Majid, a Digdol resident. FROM BANIHAL CART ROAD TO MODERN HIGHWAY Long before modern tunnels and flyovers, a steep cart road through Banihal connected Kashmir with Jammu. The Jawahar Tunnel, opened in 1956, later became the main passage through the mountains. Earlier known as NH-1A, the Srinagar-Jammu National Highway was maintained by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) before the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) took over in the early 2000s. Renumbered NH-44, it underwent a major upgrade, with four-laning beginning in phases in 2011 and a five-year completion target. The project was divided into six sub-projects: Srinagar-Qazigund (67.7 km), Qazigund-Banihal (15.25 km), Banihal-Ramban (36 km), Ramban-Udhampur (43 km), Chenani-Nashri (9.2 km), and Jammu-Udhampur (65 km). It aimed to shorten the journey by more than 50 km and cut travel time from nine hours to four. Land acquisition, utility shifting, work stoppages, difficult terrain and slow execution delayed the project, with several deadlines missed, particularly along the Ramban-Banihal stretch. Widening initially relied heavily on cutting into mountain slopes. Frequent rockfalls, landslides and slope instability, however, prompted a shift towards tunnels, bypasses, flyovers, and protective structures. Before the upgrade, heavy snowfall and rain often closed the highway, stranding passengers and trucks carrying essentials and fruit along the Banihal-Ramban-Chenani corridor for days. Until rail services reached Kashmir, the highway remained the Valley's only surface link with Jammu and the rest of the country. "Avalanches and snow used to stop travel, sometimes for days together," recalled Mushtaq Ahmad Bhat, 65, from Anantnag, who travelled to Aligarh Muslim University in 1980 for postgraduate studies in sociology.
